arXiv:1308.6623v2 [nlin.SI] 03 Sep 2013

Exact solutions of multicomponent nonlinear Schrödinger equations under general plane-wave boundary conditions

Takayuki Tsuchida
Abstract

We construct exact soliton solutions of integrable multicomponent nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equations under general nonvanishing boundary conditions. Different components of the vector (or matrix) dependent variable can approach plane waves with different wavenumbers and frequencies at spatial infinity. We apply Bäcklund–Darboux transformations to the cubic NLS equations with a self-focusing nonlinearity, a self-defocusing nonlinearity or a mixed focusing-defocusing nonlinearity. Both bright-soliton solutions and dark-soliton solutions are obtained, depending on the signs of the nonlinear terms and the type of Bäcklund–Darboux transformation. The multicomponent solitons generally possess internal degrees of freedom and provide highly nontrivial generalizations of the scalar NLS solitons. The main step in the construction of the multicomponent solitons is to compute the matrix exponential of a constant non-diagonal matrix arising from the Lax pair. With a suitable re-parametrization of the non-diagonal matrix, the matrix exponential can be computed explicitly in closed form for the most interesting cases such as the two-component vector NLS equation. In particular, we do not resort to Cardano’s formula in diagonalizing a 3×33\times 3 matrix, so our expressions for the multicomponent solitons are in some sense more explicit and useful than those obtained in [Q-H. Park and H. J. Shin, Phys. Rev. E 61 (2000) 3093].

Keywords: vector/matrix NLS, Lax pair, bright solitons, dark solitons, multicomponent solitons, Bäcklund–Darboux transformations

1 Introduction

The cubic nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation in 1+11+1 dimensions was first solved by the inverse scattering method11 1 The inverse scattering method was originally devised to solve the KdV equation[4]. under vanishing boundary conditions at spatial infinity [1, 2, 3]. The method was soon generalized to integrate the NLS equation under nonvanishing (or plane-wave22 2 The Galilean invariance of the NLS equation [12] allows us to set the wavenumber of the background plane wave as zero without loss of generality. However, the complex phase of the dependent variable can take different values for x→−∞x\to-\infty and x→+∞x\to+\infty [5, 7]. ) boundary conditions at infinity and various interesting solutions were obtained [5, 6, 7, 8] (also see [9, 10, 11]). In particular, dark-soliton solutions for the NLS equation with a self-defocusing nonlinearity [5, 13, 14, 15] and bright-soliton solutions on a plane-wave background for the NLS equation with a self-focusing nonlinearity [6, 7, 8] are the most relevant and fundamental.

The integrability of the NLS equation is based on its Lax-pair33 3 The term “Lax pair” is named after the work of Peter Lax on the KdV hierarchy [16]. (or zero-curvature) representation [1, 5, 2, 3], which provides a starting point for applying the inverse scattering method. By generalizing the Lax pair, we can straightforwardly obtain a vector/matrix analog of the NLS equation [17, 18] (also see [19]), which can be solved by the inverse scattering method under the vanishing boundary conditions. Thus, it is natural to expect that the inverse scattering method is also applicable to the vector/matrix NLS equation under general nonvanishing boundary conditions. However, in fact this is not the case. The main difficulty is that the background plane waves can have different wavenumbers and frequencies in different components of the vector/matrix dependent variable [20, 21, 22, 23]. Such a general case is not amenable to the usual formulation of the inverse scattering method [22], so only a degenerate case in which all the components approach the same plane wave at spatial infinity, up to (possibly zero) proportionality factors, has been considered [24, 25, 26, 27] (also see [28]). Although some soliton solutions in the degenerate case are certainly nontrivial and interesting [24, 29, 30, 31], they form a rather restricted subclass of the general soliton solutions satisfying the plane-wave boundary conditions.

The main objective of this paper is to construct new soliton solutions of the vector/matrix NLS equation, which have not been presented explicitly in the literature. To deal with the non-degenerate case of the nonvanishing boundary conditions involving more than one background plane wave, we use Bäcklund–Darboux transformations [32, 33] instead of the inverse scattering method. The main advantage of the Bäcklund–Darboux transformations is that a new solution of the nonlinear equation considered can be constructed from a known solution using only linear operations. More specifically, we need to find a linear eigenfunction of the Lax-pair representation for a given seed solution of the nonlinear equation. In essence, this task is equivalent to solving a linear system of ordinary differential equations in the spatial variable. For the vector/matrix NLS equation under the general plane-wave boundary conditions, the construction of soliton solutions reduces to the computation of the exponential of a constant non-diagonal matrix arising from the Lax pair [34, 35]; this also applies for the higher flows of the vector/matrix NLS hierarchy (cf. [36]). A straightforward way to compute the matrix exponential is to diagonalize the non-diagonal matrix by solving its characteristic equation.44 4 In this paper, we do not separately discuss the non-generic case wherein this non-diagonal matrix cannot be diagonalized, i.e., it has a non-diagonal Jordan normal form (cf. [37]). However, even in the simplest nontrivial case of the two-component vector NLS equation, it requires to solve a cubic equation with generally complex coefficients using Cardano’s formula55 5 The formula for finding the roots of a cubic equation has a rather complicated history (see, e.g., http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_function).  [34, 38] (also see [22]). Unfortunately, the obtained expression for the matrix exponential is too cumbersome and not suitable for investigating the asymptotic behaviors of the solutions. Moreover, such an expression intrinsically has an ambiguity, because Cardano’s formula generally involves the square and cubic roots of a complex number, which are not uniquely determined. To fix this shortcoming, we re-parametrize the non-diagonal matrix so that the matrix exponential can be computed in a more easy-to-read form without any ambiguity. Consequently, for the two-component vector NLS equation, we can express the general one-soliton solution explicitly by using the solutions of a quadratic equation with real coefficients.

The nature and the solution space of the integrable NLS equation depend critically on the sign of the cubic term. In the scalar case, there exist only two choices corresponding to the self-focusing NLS and the self-defocusing NLS, respectively; these names can be justified by considering the physical meaning of the potential energy term in the canonical Hamiltonian formalism [39]. In the multicomponent case, e.g., when the dependent variable is vector- or matrix-valued [17, 18], we have the third possibility: a mixed focusing-defocusing nonlinearity that contains both terms with a plus sign and terms with a minus sign [40, 41, 42, 20, 29, 21, 43].

In the scalar case, the self-defocusing NLS equation admits dark-soliton solutions. A dark soliton is a dip of the density in the background plane wave, which can be obtained by applying an elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation [44, 45] to the plane-wave solution. Each dark soliton is associated with a square-integrable eigenfunction (i.e., a bound state) of the Lax pair with a real eigenvalue, because the spatial Lax operator for the self-defocusing NLS equation is self-adjoint [5, 2, 3]. In contrast, the self-focusing NLS equation admits bright-soliton solutions. A bright soliton is generally a hump of the density, which can be obtained by applying a binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation [32, 33] (also see [47, 46, 48]) that is equivalent to a suitable composition of two elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformations [44, 45]. Each bright soliton is associated with two bound states of the Lax pair, wherein the spatial Lax operator is not self-adjoint and the bound-state eigenvalues form a complex conjugate pair [1, 3].

In a similar way, we can obtain multicomponent dark-soliton solutions in the self-defocusing case and multicomponent bright-soliton solutions in the self-focusing case using an elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation and a binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation, respectively. Indeed, the general formulation of the Bäcklund–Darboux transformations is valid irrespective of the matrix size of the Lax-pair representation [49, 34, 50, 35], which is related to the number of components of the vector/matrix dependent variable. A vector dark soliton [22] in the self-defocusing case does not admit any essential parameter representing the internal degrees of freedom, although it provides a nontrivial generalization of the scalar dark soliton. Contrastingly, a matrix dark soliton in the self-defocusing case and a vector/matrix bright soliton in the self-focusing case contain free parameters representing the internal degrees of freedom. The case of a mixed focusing-defocusing nonlinearity is more complicated, because it admits both a dark soliton [20, 21, 22] and a bright soliton [22]; they can be obtained by applying an elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation and a binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation, respectively. Moreover, in this case, we can also consider a limiting case of the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation in such a way that the associated two bound-state eigenvalues coalesce into a real eigenvalue (cf. §2.4 in [33] and [35]); as a result of its application, a vector dark soliton with internal degrees of freedom can be constructed. In particular, the three-component vector NLS equation with one focusing and two defocusing components admits a non-stationary dark soliton that exhibits a soliton mutation phenomenon; that is, the shape and velocity of the dark soliton can change spontaneously in the time evolution.

In the multicomponent case, it is generally impossible to distinguish between a dark soliton and a bright soliton in a rigorous manner just by looking at their wave profiles. Indeed, each soliton may exhibit a rather complicated behavior in individual components [30, 34, 50, 31], which cannot be identified as a simple dip or hump. In addition, there exists a group of linear transformations, called the symmetry group, which mixes the components of the vector/matrix dependent variable but leaves the equation of motion invariant [29, 21, 51]; for example, the self-focusing/defocusing vector NLS equation is invariant under the group of (special) unitary transformations. Such linear transformations can drastically change both the boundary conditions and the wave profile of a soliton observed in individual components. Thus, instead of distinguishing between a dark soliton and a bright soliton intuitively, in this paper we use these terms in correspondence with the type of Bäcklund–Darboux transformation generating each soliton solution. That is, in analogy with the case of the scalar NLS equation, a dark soliton is associated with a square-integrable eigenfunction of the Lax pair with a real eigenvalue, while a bright soliton entails a pair of bound states with eigenvalues that are complex conjugates of each other. Note that this definition is more stringent than that commonly used in the literature. In particular, the spatial Lax operator for the vector/matrix NLS equation with a self-defocusing nonlinearity is self-adjoint [26, 27], so it does not admit any bright-soliton solution. This is in contrast to the work of Park and Shin [34, 50], wherein they applied a binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation to the two-component vector NLS equation with a self-defocusing nonlinearity and constructed “dark-bright” and “dark-dark” soliton solutions (cf. “double solitons” in [22]). Their solutions are not associated with square-integrable eigenfunctions of the Lax pair, so we call them “soliton-like” solutions, which are not genuine soliton solutions in our definition.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we introduce step by step three types of Bäcklund–Darboux transformations for the vector/matrix NLS system. First, we introduce two elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformations on the basis of the Lax-pair representation and its adjoint problem. Second, we combine the two elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformations to define a binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation. Third, we consider a limiting case of the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation in such a way that the associated two eigenvalues merge into a single eigenvalue. In section 3, by applying an elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation to a general plane-wave solution, we obtain dark-soliton solutions of the multicomponent NLS equations with a self-defocusing or mixed focusing-defocusing nonlinearity. In section 4, we apply the limiting case of the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation to the vector NLS equation with a mixed focusing-defocusing nonlinearity. Thus, we obtain a dark-soliton solution with internal degrees of freedom, which is more general than the vector dark-soliton solution obtained in section 3. In section 5, using the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation, we construct bright-soliton solutions on a general plane-wave background for the multicomponent NLS equations with a self-focusing or mixed focusing-defocusing nonlinearity; a “soliton-like” solution in the self-defocusing case given in [34] (also see [50]) can also be obtained in a more explicit form. The last section, section 6, is devoted to concluding remarks.

2 General formulation of Bäcklund–Darboux transformations

In this section, we formulate three types of Bäcklund–Darboux transformations for the vector/matrix NLS system using the Lax-pair representation and its adjoint problem.

2.1 Multicomponent NLS systems

The matrix generalization [18] of the nonreduced NLS system [2, 3] is given by

i​Qt+Qx​x−2​Q​R​Q=O,\displaystyle{}\mathrm{i}Q_{t}+Q_{xx}-2QRQ=O, (2.1a)
i​Rt−Rx​x+2​R​Q​R=O.\displaystyle\mathrm{i}R_{t}-R_{xx}+2RQR=O. (2.1b)

Here, QQ and RR are l×ml\times m and m×lm\times l matrices, respectively, and the subscripts tt and xx denote the partial differentiation; we use the symbol OO instead of 00 to stress that the dependent variables can take their values in matrices. A list of references on the matrix NLS system (2.1b) and related equations can be found in [52].

Note that (2.1b) allows a Hermitian conjugation reduction [21] (also see [40, 41, 42, 29, 43]):

R=Σ​Q†​Ω.R=\Sigma\hskip 1.0ptQ^{\dagger}\hskip 1.0pt\Omega. (2.2)

Here, Σ\Sigma and Ω\Omega are m×mm\times m and l×ll\times l constant Hermitian matrices, respectively, and the dagger denotes the Hermitian conjugation. The reduction (2.2) simplifies the nonreduced matrix NLS system (2.1b) to the matrix NLS equation:

i​Qt+Qx​x−2​Q​Σ​Q†​Ω​Q=O.\mathrm{i}Q_{t}+Q_{xx}-2Q\Sigma\hskip 1.0ptQ^{\dagger}\hskip 1.0pt\Omega Q=O. (2.3)

Considering a linear transformation Q→U1​Q​U2Q\to U_{1}QU_{2} with nonsingular constant matrices U1U_{1} and U2U_{2}, we can recast Σ\Sigma and Ω\Omega in their canonical forms, i.e., diagonal matrices whose diagonal entries are +1+1, −1-1 or 00. Because we are more interested in truly coupled systems than in triangular systems, we require that the diagonal entries of (the canonical forms of) Σ\Sigma and Ω\Omega are +1+1 or −1-1. In particular, in the subsequent sections, we mainly consider the following two cases.

  • •

    The case l=1l=1: vector NLS equation [40, 41, 42, 29, 21, 43],

    i​𝒒t+𝒒x​x−2​⟨𝒒​Σ,𝒒∗⟩​𝒒=𝟎,\mathrm{i}\mbox{\boldmath$q$}_{t}+\mbox{\boldmath$q$}_{xx}-2\langle\mbox{\boldmath$q$}\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$q$}^{\ast}\rangle\mbox{\boldmath$q$}=\mbox{\boldmath$0$}, (2.4)

    which generalizes the Manakov model [17]. Here, 𝒒:=(q1,q2,…,qm)\mbox{\boldmath$q$}:=(q_{1},q_{2},\ldots,q_{m}) is an mm-component row vector and Σ:=diag⁡(σ1,σ2,…,σm)\Sigma:=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{m}) is a diagonal matrix with entries σj=+1\sigma_{j}=+1 or −1-1. Thus, after a suitable re-numbering of the components, the scalar product can be written explicitly as

    ⟨𝒒​Σ,𝒒∗⟩:=∑j=1n|qj|2−∑k=n+1m|qk|2,\langle\mbox{\boldmath$q$}\Sigma,\mbox{\boldmath$q$}^{\ast}\rangle:=\sum_{j=1}^{n}|q_{j}|^{2}-\sum_{k=n+1}^{m}|q_{k}|^{2},

    where n⁡(0≤n≤m)n\;(0\leq n\leq m) is the number of defocusing components and m−nm-n is the number of focusing components.

  • •

    The case l=ml=m: square matrix NLS equation [18],

    i​Qt+Qx​x−2​σ​Q​Q†​Q=O,σ=+1​or​−1.\mathrm{i}Q_{t}+Q_{xx}-2\sigma QQ^{\dagger}Q=O,\hskip 14.22636pt\sigma=+1\;\,\mbox{or}\;\,\mbox{$-1$}. (2.5)

    Here, the choice of σ=+1\sigma=+1 and the choice of σ=−1\sigma=-1 correspond to the self-defocusing case and the self-focusing case, respectively.

2.2 Lax-pair representation and Miura maps

The Lax-pair representation [16] for the nonreduced matrix NLS system (2.1b) is given by [54, 53]

[Ψ1Ψ2]x=[−i​ζ​IlQRi​ζ​Im]​[Ψ1Ψ2],\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]_{x}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-\mathrm{i}\zeta I_{l}&Q\\ R&\mathrm{i}\zeta I_{m}\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right],
[Ψ1Ψ2]t=[−2​i​ζ2​Il−i​Q​R2​ζ​Q+i​Qx2​ζ​R−i​Rx2​i​ζ2​Im+i​R​Q]​[Ψ1Ψ2].\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]_{t}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-2\mathrm{i}\zeta^{2}I_{l}-\mathrm{i}QR&2\zeta Q+\mathrm{i}Q_{x}\\ 2\zeta R-\mathrm{i}R_{x}&2\mathrm{i}\zeta^{2}I_{m}+\mathrm{i}RQ\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right].

Here, ζ\zeta is the spectral parameter, which is an arbitrary constant, and IlI_{l} and ImI_{m} are the l×ll\times l and m×mm\times m identity matrices, respectively. The compatibility condition for the overdetermined linear system (2.6) indeed implies (2.1b). Note that (2.6) can be rewritten explicitly as an eigenvalue problem [1, 5]:

[i∂x−i​Qi​R−i∂x]​[Ψ1Ψ2]=ζ⁡[Ψ1Ψ2].\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathrm{i}\partial_{x}&-\mathrm{i}Q\\ \mathrm{i}R&-\mathrm{i}\partial_{x}\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]=\zeta\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right].

In the self-defocusing case R=Q†R=Q^{\dagger}, this eigenvalue problem is self-adjoint, so the eigenvalue ζ\zeta is restricted to be real-valued for any square-integrable (i.e., bound-state) eigenfunction; note that

∫−∞∞[Ψ1†Ψ2†]​[i∂x−i​Qi​Q†−i∂x]​[Ψ1Ψ2]​𝑑x=ζ​∫−∞∞[Ψ1†Ψ2†]​[Ψ1Ψ2]​𝑑x.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Psi_{1}^{\dagger}&\!\Psi_{2}^{\dagger}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathrm{i}\partial_{x}&-\mathrm{i}Q\\ \mathrm{i}Q^{\dagger}&-\mathrm{i}\partial_{x}\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]\mathrm{d}x=\zeta\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Psi_{1}^{\dagger}&\!\Psi_{2}^{\dagger}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]\mathrm{d}x.

We also consider the adjoint Lax-pair representation:66 6 If we have a square-matrix solution Ψ\Psi of the linear system Ψx=U​Ψ,Ψt=V​Ψ\Psi_{x}=U\Psi,\;\Psi_{t}=V\Psi, then its inverse Φ:=Ψ−1\Phi:=\Psi^{-1} solves the adjoint system Φx=−Φ​U,Φt=−Φ​V\Phi_{x}=-\Phi U,\;\Phi_{t}=-\Phi V [42, 55].

[Φ1Φ2]x=−[Φ1Φ2]​[−i​ζ​IlQRi​ζ​Im],\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]_{x}=-\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-\mathrm{i}\zeta I_{l}&Q\\ R&\mathrm{i}\zeta I_{m}\\ \end{array}\right],
[Φ1Φ2]t=−[Φ1Φ2]​[−2​i​ζ2​Il−i​Q​R2​ζ​Q+i​Qx2​ζ​R−i​Rx2​i​ζ2​Im+i​R​Q].\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]_{t}=-\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-2\mathrm{i}\zeta^{2}I_{l}-\mathrm{i}QR&2\zeta Q+\mathrm{i}Q_{x}\\ 2\zeta R-\mathrm{i}R_{x}&2\mathrm{i}\zeta^{2}I_{m}+\mathrm{i}RQ\\ \end{array}\right].

Indeed, a Lagrange-like identity,

[Φ1Φ2]​{[Ψ1Ψ2]x−[−i​ζ​IlQRi​ζ​Im]​[Ψ1Ψ2]}\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]\left\{\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]_{x}-\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-\mathrm{i}\zeta I_{l}&Q\\ R&\mathrm{i}\zeta I_{m}\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]\right\}
+{[Φ1Φ2]x+[Φ1Φ2]​[−i​ζ​IlQRi​ζ​Im]}​[Ψ1Ψ2]\displaystyle\mbox{}+\left\{\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]_{x}+\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-\mathrm{i}\zeta I_{l}&Q\\ R&\mathrm{i}\zeta I_{m}\\ \end{array}\right]\right\}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]
={[Φ1Φ2]​[Ψ1Ψ2]}x,\displaystyle=\left\{\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]\right\}_{x},

and a similar relation for the tt-differentiation imply that (2.7) is the adjoint problem of (2.6). In particular, the product of solutions of (2.7) and (2.6) is (x,t)(x,t)-independent:

[Φ1Φ2]​[Ψ1Ψ2]=const.\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]=\mathrm{const.} (2.24)

We consider an (l+m)×l(l+m)\times l matrix-valued linear eigenfunction of the Lax-pair representation (2.6) such that Ψ1\Psi_{1} is an l×ll\times l nonsingular matrix and define an m×lm\times l matrix R~\widetilde{R} as R~:=Ψ2​Ψ1−1\widetilde{R}:=\Psi_{2}\Psi_{1}^{-1}. Then, (2.6) implies the relations (cf. [47, 56, 48]):

R=R~x−2​i​ζ​R~+R~​Q​R~,\displaystyle R=\widetilde{R}_{x}-2\mathrm{i}\zeta\widetilde{R}+\widetilde{R}Q\widetilde{R}, (2.25a)
R~t=2​ζ​R−i​Rx+4​i​ζ2​R~+i​R​Q​R~+i​R~​Q​R−2​ζ​R~​Q​R~−i​R~​Qx​R~.\displaystyle\widetilde{R}_{t}=2\zeta R-\mathrm{i}R_{x}+4\mathrm{i}\zeta^{2}\widetilde{R}+\mathrm{i}RQ\widetilde{R}+\mathrm{i}\widetilde{R}QR-2\zeta\widetilde{R}Q\widetilde{R}-\mathrm{i}\widetilde{R}Q_{x}\widetilde{R}. (2.25b)

Relation (2.25a) enables us to express RR in (2.1a) and (2.25b) in terms of QQ and R~\widetilde{R} [57]. Thus, we obtain a closed two-component system for QQ and R~\widetilde{R}:

i​Qt+Qx​x+4​i​ζ​Q​R~​Q−2​Q​R~x​Q−2​Q​R~​Q​R~​Q=O,\displaystyle{}\mathrm{i}Q_{t}+Q_{xx}+4\mathrm{i}\zeta Q\widetilde{R}Q-2Q\widetilde{R}_{x}Q-2Q\widetilde{R}Q\widetilde{R}Q=O, (2.26a)
i​R~t−R~x​x−4​i​ζ​R~​Q​R~−2​R~​Qx​R~+2​R~​Q​R~​Q​R~=O.\displaystyle\mathrm{i}\widetilde{R}_{t}-\widetilde{R}_{xx}-4\mathrm{i}\zeta\widetilde{R}Q\widetilde{R}-2\widetilde{R}Q_{x}\widetilde{R}+2\widetilde{R}Q\widetilde{R}Q\widetilde{R}=O. (2.26b)

This is a matrix generalization [58, 59, 60, 61, 62, 63] of the derivative NLS system studied by Ablowitz, Ramani and Segur [64] (and later by Gerdjikov and Ivanov [65] without citing the paper [64]); the cubic terms involving the parameter ζ\zeta can be removed by a simple point transformation (cf. [66, 67, 68]). Note that (2.25a) defines a Miura map from (2.26b) to (2.1b): (Q,R~)↦(Q,R)(Q,\widetilde{R})\mapsto(Q,R).

Similarly, using a linear eigenfunction of the adjoint Lax-pair representation (2.7), we define an l×ml\times m matrix Q^\widehat{Q} as Q^:=Φ1−1​Φ2\widehat{Q}:=\Phi_{1}^{-1}\Phi_{2}. Then, we obtain the relations:

Q=−Q^x−2​i​ζ​Q^+Q^​R​Q^,\displaystyle Q=-\widehat{Q}_{x}-2\mathrm{i}\zeta\widehat{Q}+\widehat{Q}R\widehat{Q}, (2.27a)
Q^t=−2​ζ​Q−i​Qx−4​i​ζ2​Q^−i​Q​R​Q^−i​Q^​R​Q+2​ζ​Q^​R​Q^−i​Q^​Rx​Q^.\displaystyle\widehat{Q}_{t}=-2\zeta Q-\mathrm{i}Q_{x}-4\mathrm{i}\zeta^{2}\widehat{Q}-\mathrm{i}QR\widehat{Q}-\mathrm{i}\widehat{Q}RQ+2\zeta\widehat{Q}R\widehat{Q}-\mathrm{i}\widehat{Q}R_{x}\widehat{Q}. (2.27b)

Relation (2.27a) allows us to express QQ in (2.27b) and (2.1b) in terms of Q^\widehat{Q} and RR. Thus, a closed system for Q^\widehat{Q} and RR is obtained:

i​Q^t+Q^x​x+4​i​ζ​Q^​R​Q^−2​Q^​Rx​Q^−2​Q^​R​Q^​R​Q^=O,\displaystyle{}\mathrm{i}\widehat{Q}_{t}+\widehat{Q}_{xx}+4\mathrm{i}\zeta\widehat{Q}R\widehat{Q}-2\widehat{Q}R_{x}\widehat{Q}-2\widehat{Q}R\widehat{Q}R\widehat{Q}=O, (2.28a)
i​Rt−Rx​x−4​i​ζ​R​Q^​R−2​R​Q^x​R+2​R​Q^​R​Q^​R=O.\displaystyle\mathrm{i}R_{t}-R_{xx}-4\mathrm{i}\zeta R\widehat{Q}R-2R\widehat{Q}_{x}R+2R\widehat{Q}R\widehat{Q}R=O. (2.28b)

Note that (2.26b) and (2.28b) are identical, so we have another Miura map (2.27a) from (2.28b) to (2.1b): (Q^,R)↦(Q,R)(\widehat{Q},R)\mapsto(Q,R).

2.3 Elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformations

We have obtained two distinct Miura maps from the matrix derivative NLS system to the matrix NLS system [68, 59]; the inverse of each Miura map can be expressed in terms of a linear eigenfunction of the (adjoint) Lax-pair representation for the matrix NLS system. Thus, combining the inverse of one Miura map with the other Miura map, we can construct an elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation for the matrix NLS system. Moreover, we can also identify the gauge transformation of the linear eigenfunction of the Lax-pair representation, which generates each elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation [69, 70, 71]. In the following, we often fix the arbitrary parameter ζ\zeta in the Bäcklund–Darboux transformation at some specific value, say ζ=μ\zeta=\mu, to distinguish it from the original spectral parameter ζ\zeta in the Lax-pair representation.

Proposition 2.1.

The spatial part of an elementary auto-Bäcklund transformation for the matrix NLS system (2.1b), which connects two solutions (Q,R)(Q,R) and (Q~,R~)(\widetilde{Q},\widetilde{R}), is given by (see [44, 45] for the scalar case and [59, 71] for the matrix case)

Q~=−Qx−2​i​μ​Q+Q​R~​Q,\displaystyle\widetilde{Q}=-Q_{x}-2\mathrm{i}\mu Q+Q\widetilde{R}Q,
R=R~x−2​i​μ​R~+R~​Q​R~.\displaystyle R=\widetilde{R}_{x}-2\mathrm{i}\mu\widetilde{R}+\widetilde{R}Q\widetilde{R}.

The transformation (Q,R)↦(Q~,R~)(Q,R)\mapsto(\widetilde{Q},\widetilde{R}) can be expressed explicitly in terms of a linear eigenfunction of the Lax-pair representation (2.6) at ζ=μ\zeta=\mu as [44, 45]

R~=Ψ2​Ψ1−1|ζ=μ,Q~=−Qx−2​i​μ​Q+Q​R~​Q.\widetilde{R}=\left.\Psi_{2}\Psi_{1}^{-1}\right|_{\zeta=\mu},\hskip 14.22636pt\widetilde{Q}=-Q_{x}-2\mathrm{i}\mu Q+Q\widetilde{R}Q. (2.29)

The corresponding gauge transformation [69, 70, 71],

[Ψ~1Ψ~2]:=G⁡(Q,R~,μ)​[Ψ1Ψ2],G⁡(Q,R~,μ):=g⁡(ζ,μ)​[2​i​(ζ−μ)​Il+Q​R~−Q−R~Im],\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\widetilde{\Psi}_{1}\\ \widetilde{\Psi}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]:=G(Q,\widetilde{R};\mu)\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right],\hskip 14.22636ptG(Q,\widetilde{R};\mu):=g(\zeta,\mu)\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}2\mathrm{i}(\zeta-\mu)I_{l}+Q\widetilde{R}&-Q\\ -\widetilde{R}&I_{m}\\ \end{array}\right],

where gg is an arbitrary (but not identically zero) scalar function of ζ\zeta and μ\mu, changes the original Lax-pair representation (2.6) with R=R~x−2​i​μ​R~+R~​Q​R~R=\widetilde{R}_{x}-2\mathrm{i}\mu\widetilde{R}+\widetilde{R}Q\widetilde{R} into a new Lax-pair representation of the same form. That is,

[Ψ~1Ψ~2]x=[−i​ζ​IlQ~R~i​ζ​Im]​[Ψ~1Ψ~2],Q~=−Qx−2​i​μ​Q+Q​R~​Q,\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\widetilde{\Psi}_{1}\\ \widetilde{\Psi}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]_{x}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-\mathrm{i}\zeta I_{l}&\widetilde{Q}\\ \widetilde{R}&\mathrm{i}\zeta I_{m}\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\widetilde{\Psi}_{1}\\ \widetilde{\Psi}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right],\hskip 14.22636pt\widetilde{Q}=-Q_{x}-2\mathrm{i}\mu Q+Q\widetilde{R}Q,

and similar for the tt-differentiation. In the same manner, the gauge transformation preserving the form of the adjoint Lax-pair representation (2.7) is given by

[Φ~1Φ~2]:=[Φ1Φ2]​H​(Q,R~,μ),H⁡(Q,R~,μ):=h⁡(ζ,μ)​[IlQR~2​i​(ζ−μ)​Im+R~​Q],\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\widetilde{\Phi}_{1}&\!\widetilde{\Phi}_{2}\end{array}\right]:=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]H(Q,\widetilde{R};\mu),\hskip 14.22636ptH(Q,\widetilde{R};\mu):=h(\zeta,\mu)\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}I_{l}&Q\\ \widetilde{R}&2\mathrm{i}(\zeta-\mu)I_{m}+\widetilde{R}Q\\ \end{array}\right],

where hh is an arbitrary (but not identically zero) scalar function of ζ\zeta and μ\mu. Note that G⁡(Q,R~,μ)​H​(Q,R~,μ)=2​i​(ζ−μ)​g​(ζ,μ)​h​(ζ,μ)​Il+mG(Q,\widetilde{R};\mu)H(Q,\widetilde{R};\mu)=2\mathrm{i}(\zeta-\mu)g(\zeta,\mu)h(\zeta,\mu)I_{l+m}.

The elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation (Q,R)↦(Q~,R~)(Q,R)\mapsto(\widetilde{Q},\widetilde{R}) defined by (2.29) is not a map determining (Q~,R~)(\widetilde{Q},\widetilde{R}) uniquely; indeed, it involves additional free parameters, because each column of the linear eigenfunction used in (2.29) is an arbitrary linear combination of a fundamental set of solutions. The transformation admits the following conservation law:

Q~​R~−Q​R\displaystyle\widetilde{Q}\widetilde{R}-QR =−(Q​R~)x\displaystyle=-\left(Q\widetilde{R}\right)_{x}
=−(Q​Ψ2​Ψ1−1|ζ=μ)x\displaystyle=-\left(Q\left.\Psi_{2}\Psi_{1}^{-1}\right|_{\zeta=\mu}\right)_{x}
=−(Ψ1,x​Ψ1−1|ζ=μ)x.\displaystyle=-\left(\left.\Psi_{1,x}\Psi_{1}^{-1}\right|_{\zeta=\mu}\right)_{x}.

Thus, if we can choose the linear eigenfunction such that limx→−∞Ψ1,x​Ψ1−1\lim_{x\to-\infty}\Psi_{1,x}\Psi_{1}^{-1} and limx→+∞Ψ1,x​Ψ1−1\lim_{x\to+\infty}\Psi_{1,x}\Psi_{1}^{-1} exist and Ψ1,x​Ψ1−1\Psi_{1,x}\Psi_{1}^{-1} does not oscillate extraordinarily rapidly as x→±∞x\to\pm\infty, then Q~​R~\widetilde{Q}\widetilde{R} and Q​RQR exhibit the same asymptotic behavior at spatial infinity. In addition, there exists another conservation law:

R~​Q~−R​Q\displaystyle\widetilde{R}\widetilde{Q}-RQ =−(R~​Q)x\displaystyle=-\left(\widetilde{R}Q\right)_{x}
=−(Ψ2​Ψ1−1|ζ=μ​Q)x.\displaystyle=-\left(\left.\Psi_{2}\Psi_{1}^{-1}\right|_{\zeta=\mu}Q\right)_{x}.

These conservation laws give a useful hint on how to realize a Hermitian conjugation reduction between Q~\widetilde{Q} and R~\widetilde{R}.

Combining the inverse of one Miura map with the other Miura map in the other way, we obtain another elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation; by construction, it provides the inverse of the elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation defined in Proposition 2.1 if appropriate boundary conditions are imposed (cf. [44]).

Proposition 2.2.

The spatial part of an elementary auto-Bäcklund transformation for the matrix NLS system (2.1b), which connects two solutions (Q,R)(Q,R) and (Q^,R^)(\widehat{Q},\widehat{R}), is given by (see [44, 45] for the scalar case and [59, 71] for the matrix case)

Q=−Q^x−2​i​ν​Q^+Q^​R​Q^,\displaystyle Q=-\widehat{Q}_{x}-2\mathrm{i}\nu\widehat{Q}+\widehat{Q}R\widehat{Q},
R^=Rx−2​i​ν​R+R​Q^​R.\displaystyle\widehat{R}=R_{x}-2\mathrm{i}\nu R+R\widehat{Q}R.

The transformation (Q,R)↦(Q^,R^)(Q,R)\mapsto(\widehat{Q},\widehat{R}) can be expressed explicitly in terms of a linear eigenfunction of the adjoint Lax-pair representation (2.7) at ζ=ν\zeta=\nu as

Q^=Φ1−1​Φ2|ζ=ν,R^=Rx−2​i​ν​R+R​Q^​R.\widehat{Q}=\left.\Phi_{1}^{-1}\Phi_{2}\right|_{\zeta=\nu},\hskip 14.22636pt\widehat{R}=R_{x}-2\mathrm{i}\nu R+R\widehat{Q}R.

The corresponding gauge transformation [70, 71, 69],

[Ψ^1Ψ^2]:=H⁡(Q^,R,ν)​[Ψ1Ψ2],H⁡(Q^,R,ν)=h⁡(ζ,ν)​[IlQ^R2​i​(ζ−ν)​Im+R​Q^],\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\widehat{\Psi}_{1}\\ \widehat{\Psi}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]:=H(\widehat{Q},R;\nu)\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right],\hskip 14.22636ptH(\widehat{Q},R;\nu)=h(\zeta,\nu)\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}I_{l}&\widehat{Q}\\ R&2\mathrm{i}(\zeta-\nu)I_{m}+R\widehat{Q}\\ \end{array}\right],

changes the original Lax-pair representation (2.6) with Q=−Q^x−2​i​ν​Q^+Q^​R​Q^Q=-\widehat{Q}_{x}-2\mathrm{i}\nu\widehat{Q}+\widehat{Q}R\widehat{Q} into a new Lax-pair representation of the same form. That is,

[Ψ^1Ψ^2]x=[−i​ζ​IlQ^R^i​ζ​Im]​[Ψ^1Ψ^2],R^=Rx−2​i​ν​R+R​Q^​R,\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\widehat{\Psi}_{1}\\ \widehat{\Psi}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]_{x}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-\mathrm{i}\zeta I_{l}&\widehat{Q}\\ \widehat{R}&\mathrm{i}\zeta I_{m}\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\widehat{\Psi}_{1}\\ \widehat{\Psi}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right],\hskip 14.22636pt\widehat{R}=R_{x}-2\mathrm{i}\nu R+R\widehat{Q}R,

and similar for the tt-differentiation. The gauge transformation preserving the form of the adjoint Lax-pair representation (2.7) is given by

[Φ^1Φ^2]:=[Φ1Φ2]​G​(Q^,R,ν),G⁡(Q^,R,ν)=g⁡(ζ,ν)​[2​i​(ζ−ν)​Il+Q^​R−Q^−RIm].\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\widehat{\Phi}_{1}&\!\widehat{\Phi}_{2}\end{array}\right]:=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]G(\widehat{Q},R;\nu),\hskip 14.22636ptG(\widehat{Q},R;\nu)=g(\zeta,\nu)\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}2\mathrm{i}(\zeta-\nu)I_{l}+\widehat{Q}R&-\widehat{Q}\\ -R&I_{m}\\ \end{array}\right].

aa

The elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation (Q,R)↦(Q^,R^)(Q,R)\mapsto(\widehat{Q},\widehat{R}) admits the following conservation laws:

Q^​R^−Q​R\displaystyle\widehat{Q}\widehat{R}-QR =(Q^​R)x\displaystyle=\left(\widehat{Q}R\right)_{x}
=−(Φ1−1​Φ1,x|ζ=ν)x,\displaystyle=-\left(\left.\Phi_{1}^{-1}\Phi_{1,x}\right|_{\zeta=\nu}\right)_{x},
R^​Q^−R​Q\displaystyle\widehat{R}\widehat{Q}-RQ =(R​Q^)x\displaystyle=\left(R\widehat{Q}\right)_{x}
=(R​Φ1−1​Φ2|ζ=ν)x.\displaystyle=\left(R\left.\Phi_{1}^{-1}\Phi_{2}\right|_{\zeta=\nu}\right)_{x}.

2.4 Binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation

We can further combine the two elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformations defined in Propositions 2.1 and 2.2 involving the Bäcklund parameters μ\mu and ν\nu, respectively. In the following, we consider the composition in the order

(Q,R)↦(Q~,R~)↦(Q~^,R~^)(Q,R)\mapsto(\widetilde{Q},\widetilde{R})\mapsto({\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{},{\widehat{\widetilde{R}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{}) (2.54)

because the composition in the opposite order

(Q,R)↦(Q^,R^)↦(Q^~,R^~)(Q,R)\mapsto(\widehat{Q},\widehat{R})\mapsto({\widetilde{\widehat{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{},{\widetilde{\widehat{R}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{})

provides the same final result; that is, the two elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformations commute with each other [44, 51, 72].

Thus, by applying Propositions 2.1 and 2.2 in the order (2.54), we obtain

Q~^\displaystyle{\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{} =[Φ1​(ν)+Φ2​(ν)​R~]−1​[Φ1​(ν)​Q+2​i​(ν−μ)​Φ2​(ν)+Φ2​(ν)​R~​Q]\displaystyle=\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)\widetilde{R}\right]^{-1}\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)Q+2\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)\Phi_{2}(\nu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)\widetilde{R}Q\right]
=Q+2​i​(ν−μ)​[Φ1​(ν)+Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)​Ψ1​(μ)−1]−1​Φ2​(ν)\displaystyle=Q+2\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)^{-1}\right]^{-1}\Phi_{2}(\nu)
=Q+2​i​(ν−μ)​Ψ1​(μ)​[Φ1​(ν)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)]−1​Φ2​(ν),\displaystyle=Q+2\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right]^{-1}\Phi_{2}(\nu), (2.55a)
and
R~^\displaystyle{\widehat{\widetilde{R}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{} =R~x−2​i​ν​R~+R~​Q~^​R~\displaystyle=\widetilde{R}_{x}-2\mathrm{i}\nu\widetilde{R}+\widetilde{R}{\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{}\widetilde{R}
=R−2​i​(ν−μ)​R~+R~​(Q~^−Q)​R~\displaystyle=R-2\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)\widetilde{R}+\widetilde{R}\Bigl({\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{}-Q\Bigr)\widetilde{R}
=R−2​i​(ν−μ)​Ψ2​(μ)​Ψ1​(μ)−1\displaystyle=R-2\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)^{-1}
=+2​i​(ν−μ)​Ψ2​(μ)​[Φ1​(ν)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)]−1​Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)​Ψ1​(μ)−1\displaystyle\hphantom{=}\;\,+2\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right]^{-1}\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)^{-1}
=R−2​i​(ν−μ)​Ψ2​(μ)​[Φ1​(ν)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)]−1​Φ1​(ν).\displaystyle=R-2\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right]^{-1}\Phi_{1}(\nu). (2.55b)

The corresponding gauge transformation of the linear eigenfunction can be written as

[Ψ~^1Ψ~^2]:=\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\widehat{\widetilde{\Psi}}_{1}\\ \widehat{\widetilde{\Psi}}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]:= H⁡(Q~^,R~,ν)​G​(Q,R~,μ)​[Ψ1Ψ2]\displaystyle\hskip 3.0ptH({\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{},\widetilde{R};\nu)G(Q,\widetilde{R};\mu)\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]
=\displaystyle= h⁡(ζ,ν)​g​(ζ,μ)​[IlQ~^R~2​i​(ζ−ν)​Im+R~​Q~^]​[2​i​(ζ−μ)​Il+Q​R~−Q−R~Im]​[Ψ1Ψ2]\displaystyle\hskip 3.0pth(\zeta,\nu)g(\zeta,\mu)\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}I_{l}&{\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}\\ \widetilde{R}&2\mathrm{i}(\zeta-\nu)I_{m}+\widetilde{R}{\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}2\mathrm{i}(\zeta-\mu)I_{l}+Q\widetilde{R}&-Q\\ -\widetilde{R}&I_{m}\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]
=\displaystyle= h⁡(ζ,ν)​g​(ζ,μ)​[2​i​(ζ−μ)​Il+(Q−Q~^)​R~Q~^−Q2​i​(ν−μ)​R~+R~​(Q−Q~^)​R~2​i​(ζ−ν)​Im+R~​(Q~^−Q)]​[Ψ1Ψ2]\displaystyle\hskip 3.0pth(\zeta,\nu)g(\zeta,\mu)\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}2\mathrm{i}(\zeta-\mu)I_{l}+\Bigl(Q-{\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{}\Bigr)\widetilde{R}&{\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{}-Q\\ 2\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)\widetilde{R}+\widetilde{R}\Bigl(Q-{\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{}\Bigr)\widetilde{R}&2\mathrm{i}(\zeta-\nu)I_{m}+\widetilde{R}\Bigl({\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{}-Q\Bigr)\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]
∝\displaystyle\propto {Il+m+ν−μζ−ν​[Ψ1​(μ)Ψ2​(μ)]​[Φ1​(ν)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)]−1​[Φ1​(ν)Φ2​(ν)]}​[Ψ1Ψ2].\displaystyle\hskip 1.0pt\left\{I_{l+m}+\frac{\nu-\mu}{\zeta-\nu}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}(\mu)\\ \Psi_{2}(\mu)\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right]^{-1}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}(\nu)&\!\Phi_{2}(\nu)\end{array}\right]\right\}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right].

Here, we omit the unessential proportionality factor in the last line. In a similar way, the gauge transformation of the adjoint linear eigenfunction can be written as

[Φ~^1Φ~^2]\displaystyle\hskip 1.0pt\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\widehat{\widetilde{\Phi}}_{1}&\!\widehat{\widetilde{\Phi}}_{2}\end{array}\right]
∝\displaystyle\propto [Φ1Φ2]​{Il+m+μ−νζ−μ​[Ψ1​(μ)Ψ2​(μ)]​[Φ1​(ν)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)]−1​[Φ1​(ν)Φ2​(ν)]}.\displaystyle\hskip 1.0pt\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]\left\{I_{l+m}+\frac{\mu-\nu}{\zeta-\mu}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}(\mu)\\ \Psi_{2}(\mu)\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right]^{-1}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}(\nu)&\!\Phi_{2}(\nu)\end{array}\right]\right\}.

Note that the commutativity of the two elementary Bäcklund transformations can be expressed in the matrix product form (cf. [73, 74, 75]):

[IlQ~^R~2​i​(ζ−ν)​Im+R~​Q~^]​[2​i​(ζ−μ)​Il+Q​R~−Q−R~Im]\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}I_{l}&{\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}\\ \widetilde{R}&2\mathrm{i}(\zeta-\nu)I_{m}+\widetilde{R}{\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}2\mathrm{i}(\zeta-\mu)I_{l}+Q\widetilde{R}&-Q\\ -\widetilde{R}&I_{m}\\ \end{array}\right]
=[2​i​(ζ−μ)​Il+Q^​R^~−Q^−R^~Im]​[IlQ^R2​i​(ζ−ν)​Im+R​Q^],\displaystyle=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}2\mathrm{i}(\zeta-\mu)I_{l}+\widehat{Q}{\widetilde{\widehat{R}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}&-\widehat{Q}\\ -{\widetilde{\widehat{R}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}&I_{m}\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}I_{l}&\widehat{Q}\\ R&2\mathrm{i}(\zeta-\nu)I_{m}+R\widehat{Q}\\ \end{array}\right],

which provides the nonlinear superposition principle for the solutions of the matrix NLS hierarchy. It can be described by the pair of relations [44, 45, 71]:

Q~^=Q+2​i​(ν−μ)​Q^​(Im+R~​Q^)−1,\displaystyle{\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{}=Q+2\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)\widehat{Q}\left(I_{m}+\widetilde{R}\widehat{Q}\right)^{-1},
R^~=R+2​i​(μ−ν)​R~​(Il+Q^​R~)−1.\displaystyle{\widetilde{\widehat{R}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{}=R+2\mathrm{i}(\mu-\nu)\widetilde{R}\left(I_{l}+\widehat{Q}\widetilde{R}\right)^{-1}.

These relations can be reinterpreted as a fully discrete integrable system defined on the two-dimensional lattice [69, 76, 74, 75].

The composition of the two elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformations defines a binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation [32, 33] that can be formulated as follows.

Proposition 2.3.

For a linear eigenfunction satisfying (2.6) at ζ=μ\zeta=\mu and an adjoint linear eigenfunction satisfying (2.7) at ζ=ν\zeta=\nu, we define a projection matrix P⁡(μ,ν)P(\mu,\nu) in the 2×22\times 2 block-matrix form:

P⁡(μ,ν)\displaystyle P(\mu,\nu) :=[Ψ1​(μ)Ψ2​(μ)]​[Φ1​(ν)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)]−1​[Φ1​(ν)Φ2​(ν)].\displaystyle:=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}(\mu)\\ \Psi_{2}(\mu)\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right]^{-1}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}(\nu)&\!\Phi_{2}(\nu)\end{array}\right].

Indeed, P2=PP^{2}=P. Then, the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation (Q,R)↦(Q~^,R~^)(Q,R)\mapsto({\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{},{\widehat{\widetilde{R}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{}) for the matrix NLS system (2.1b) can be expressed as (see [47, 48] for the scalar case and [49, 34, 50, 77, 38] for the vector case)

Q~^\displaystyle{\widehat{\widetilde{Q}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{} =Q+2​i​(ν−μ)​P12​(μ,ν),\displaystyle=Q+2\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)P_{12}(\mu,\nu),
R~^\displaystyle{\widehat{\widetilde{R}\mkern 3.0mu}\mkern-3.0mu}{} =R−2​i​(ν−μ)​P21​(μ,ν).\displaystyle=R-2\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)P_{21}(\mu,\nu).

Here, P12P_{12} and P21P_{21} denote the upper-right and lower-left block of the matrix PP, respectively. The corresponding gauge transformation of the linear eigenfunction is given as

[Ψ~^1Ψ~^2]∝\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\widehat{\widetilde{\Psi}}_{1}\\ \widehat{\widetilde{\Psi}}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]\propto {Il+m−μ−νζ−ν​P​(μ,ν)}​[Ψ1Ψ2],\displaystyle\left\{I_{l+m}-\frac{\mu-\nu}{\zeta-\nu}P(\mu,\nu)\right\}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right],

up to an overall constant, which coincides with the form suggested by the Zakharov–Shabat dressing method [78]. The gauge transformation of the adjoint linear eigenfunction is given using the inverse of the above dressing operator as

[Φ~^1Φ~^2]∝[Φ1Φ2]​{Il+m−ν−μζ−μ​P​(μ,ν)}.\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\widehat{\widetilde{\Phi}}_{1}&\!\widehat{\widetilde{\Phi}}_{2}\end{array}\right]\propto\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]\left\{I_{l+m}-\frac{\nu-\mu}{\zeta-\mu}P(\mu,\nu)\right\}.

In the limit ν→μ\nu\to\mu, the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation reduces to the identity transformation as long as Φ1​(μ)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(μ)​Ψ2​(μ)\Phi_{1}(\mu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\mu)\Psi_{2}(\mu) is an invertible matrix (cf. (2.24)).

Thus, under a suitable choice of the (adjoint) linear eigenfunctions used in the transformations, the two elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformations defined in Propositions 2.1 and 2.2 are the inverse of each other at μ=ν\mu=\nu. However, we can consider a more interesting choice of the (adjoint) linear eigenfunctions such that the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation reduces to a nontrivial transformation in the limit ν→μ\nu\to\mu.

2.5 Coalescence limit of the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation

From the Lax-pair representation (2.6) and its adjoint (2.7), we can show that the product of an adjoint linear eigenfunction and a linear eigenfunction satisfies (cf. [1, 3])

{1i⁡(ν−μ)​[Φ1​(ν)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)]}x=Φ1​(ν)​Ψ1​(μ)−Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)\displaystyle\left\{\frac{1}{\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)}\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right]\right\}_{x}=\Phi_{1}(\nu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)-\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)

and

{1i⁡(ν−μ)​[Φ1​(ν)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)]}t\displaystyle\left\{\frac{1}{\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)}\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right]\right\}_{t}
=\displaystyle= 2​(μ+ν)​[Φ1​(ν)​Ψ1​(μ)−Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)]+2​i​[Φ1​(ν)​Q​Ψ2​(μ)+Φ2​(ν)​R​Ψ1​(μ)].\displaystyle\hskip 3.0pt2(\mu+\nu)\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)-\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right]+2\mathrm{i}\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)Q\Psi_{2}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)R\Psi_{1}(\mu)\right].

By construction, these two relations are compatible, i.e.

{Φ1​(ν)​Ψ1​(μ)−Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)}t\displaystyle\left\{\Phi_{1}(\nu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)-\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right\}_{t}
=\displaystyle= {2​(μ+ν)​[Φ1​(ν)​Ψ1​(μ)−Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)]+2​i​[Φ1​(ν)​Q​Ψ2​(μ)+Φ2​(ν)​R​Ψ1​(μ)]}x.\displaystyle\hskip 3.0pt\left\{2(\mu+\nu)\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)-\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right]+2\mathrm{i}\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)Q\Psi_{2}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)R\Psi_{1}(\mu)\right]\right\}_{x}.

Thus, if we introduce an l×ll\times l matrix FF as

F⁡(μ):=limν→μ1i⁡(ν−μ)​[Φ1​(ν)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(ν)​Ψ2​(μ)],F(\mu):=\lim_{\nu\to\mu}\frac{1}{\mathrm{i}(\nu-\mu)}\left[\Phi_{1}(\nu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\nu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right], (2.97)

it satisfies the pair of relations:

Fx=Φ1​(μ)​Ψ1​(μ)−Φ2​(μ)​Ψ2​(μ),\displaystyle F_{x}=\Phi_{1}(\mu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)-\Phi_{2}(\mu)\Psi_{2}(\mu), (2.98a)
Ft=4​μ​Fx+2​i​[Φ1​(μ)​Q​Ψ2​(μ)+Φ2​(μ)​R​Ψ1​(μ)].\displaystyle F_{t}=4\mu F_{x}+2\mathrm{i}\left[\Phi_{1}(\mu)Q\Psi_{2}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\mu)R\Psi_{1}(\mu)\right]. (2.98b)

Moreover, F−1F^{-1} should satisfy

F−1​[Φ1​(μ)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(μ)​Ψ2​(μ)]=[Φ1​(μ)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(μ)​Ψ2​(μ)]​F−1=O.F^{-1}\left[\Phi_{1}(\mu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\mu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right]=\left[\Phi_{1}(\mu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\mu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right]F^{-1}=O.

In this paper, we consider the simplest case where Φ1​(μ)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(μ)​Ψ2​(μ)\Phi_{1}(\mu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\mu)\Psi_{2}(\mu) vanishes (cf. (2.24)). Thus, considering the ν→μ\nu\to\mu limit of Proposition 2.3, we arrive at a nontrivial limiting case of the binary Bäcklund--Darboux transformation.77 7 Such a limiting procedure is already well-known for the linear Schrödinger equation associated with the KdV equation (see §2.4 of [33]); the resulting transformation is sometimes referred to as the Abraham–Moses transformation [79] (see [80] for details). Relavant results were obtained independently by Degasperis and Lombardo [35] using a different approach.

Proposition 2.4.

We choose a linear eigenfunction and an adjoint linear eigenfunction satisfying (2.6) and (2.7), respectively, at ζ=μ\zeta=\mu in such a way that their (x,t)(x,t)-independent product is equal to zero:

Φ1​(μ)​Ψ1​(μ)+Φ2​(μ)​Ψ2​(μ)=O.\Phi_{1}(\mu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)+\Phi_{2}(\mu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)=O.

We can introduce F⁡(μ)F(\mu) that satisfies both (2.98a) and (2.98b), because they are compatible. Thus, F⁡(μ)F(\mu) is defined up to the addition of an integration constant, which is an arbitrary l×ll\times l matrix. Then, the limiting case of the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation, (Q,R)↦(Q˘,R˘)(Q,R)\mapsto(\breve{Q},\breve{R}), for the matrix NLS system (2.1b) can be expressed as

Q˘\displaystyle\breve{Q} =Q+2​𝒫12​(μ),\displaystyle=Q+2{\cal P}_{12}(\mu), (2.99a)
R˘\displaystyle\breve{R} =R−2​𝒫21​(μ).\displaystyle=R-2{\cal P}_{21}(\mu). (2.99b)

Here, 𝒫12{\cal P}_{12} and 𝒫21{\cal P}_{21} are the upper-right and lower-left block, respectively, of the nilpotent matrix 𝒫⁡(μ){\cal P}(\mu) defined as

𝒫⁡(μ)\displaystyle{\cal P}(\mu) :=[Ψ1​(μ)Ψ2​(μ)]​F​(μ)−1​[Φ1​(μ)Φ2​(μ)].\displaystyle:=\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}(\mu)\\ \Psi_{2}(\mu)\\ \end{array}\right]F(\mu)^{-1}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}(\mu)&\!\Phi_{2}(\mu)\end{array}\right].

Note that 𝒫2=O{\cal P}^{2}=O. The corresponding gauge transformation that preserves the form of the Lax-pair representation (2.6) is given as

[Ψ˘1Ψ˘2]∝\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\breve{\Psi}_{1}\\ \breve{\Psi}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]\propto {Il+m−iζ−μ​𝒫​(μ)}​[Ψ1Ψ2],\displaystyle\left\{I_{l+m}-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\zeta-\mu}{\cal P}(\mu)\right\}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right],

up to an overall constant. The gauge transformation that preserves the form of the adjoint Lax-pair representation (2.7) is given using the inverse of the above operator as

[Φ˘1Φ˘2]∝[Φ1Φ2]​{Il+m+iζ−μ​𝒫​(μ)}.\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\breve{\Phi}_{1}&\!\breve{\Phi}_{2}\end{array}\right]\propto\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Phi_{1}&\!\Phi_{2}\end{array}\right]\left\{I_{l+m}+\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\zeta-\mu}{\cal P}(\mu)\right\}.

At

The validity of Proposition 2.4 can be checked by a direct calculation. Note that F⁡(μ)F(\mu) satisfying (2.98) can be informally written as

F⁡(μ)\displaystyle F(\mu) =2​C+∫[Φ1​(μ)​Ψ1​(μ)−Φ2​(μ)​Ψ2​(μ)]​𝑑x\displaystyle=2C+\int\left[\Phi_{1}(\mu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)-\Phi_{2}(\mu)\Psi_{2}(\mu)\right]\mathrm{d}x
=2​[C+∫Φ1​(μ)​Ψ1​(μ)​𝑑x],\displaystyle=2\left[C+\int\Phi_{1}(\mu)\Psi_{1}(\mu)\hskip 1.0pt\mathrm{d}x\right],

where CC is an arbitrary l×ll\times l constant matrix. More precisely, the time independence of CC should be checked by using (2.98b); however, this process can be skipped by choosing the linear eigenfunction and the adjoint linear eigenfunction so that the right-hand sides of (2.98a) and (2.98b) decay rapidly as x→−∞x\to-\infty (or +∞+\infty). This expression involves one integration, but it is generally much easier to compute than taking the limit following the original definition (2.97) (cf. [34, 81]).

2.6 Seed solution

A general plane-wave solution of the nonreduced matrix NLS system (2.1b) is given by

Q=P1​e−2​i​t​A​B​A​ei​x​Γ−i​t​Γ2​P2,R=P2−1​e−i​x​Γ+i​t​Γ2​B​e2​i​t​A​B​P1−1,\displaystyle Q=P_{1}\mathrm{e}^{-2\mathrm{i}tAB}A\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}x\Gamma-\mathrm{i}t\Gamma^{2}}P_{2},\hskip 14.22636ptR=P_{2}^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}x\Gamma+\mathrm{i}t\Gamma^{2}}B\mathrm{e}^{2\mathrm{i}tAB}P_{1}^{-1}, (2.109)

where Γ\Gamma, AA, BB, P1P_{1} and P2P_{2} are constant matrices; P1P_{1} is an l×ll\times l matrix, Γ\Gamma and P2P_{2} are m×mm\times m matrices, AA is an l×ml\times m matrix and BB is an m×lm\times l matrix. Actually, P1P_{1} and P2P_{2} can be removed by redefining Γ\Gamma, AA and BB; note, however, that they can be used to cast Γ\Gamma and A​BAB in Jordan normal form. A general plane-wave solution of the matrix NLS equation (2.3) can be obtained by imposing the reduction conditions

P1†​Ω​P1=Ω,P2​Σ​P2†=Σ,Σ​Γ†​Σ−1=Γ,B=Σ​A†​ΩP_{1}^{\dagger}\Omega P_{1}=\Omega,\hskip 14.22636ptP_{2}\Sigma P_{2}^{\dagger}=\Sigma,\hskip 14.22636pt\Sigma\Gamma^{\dagger}\Sigma^{-1}=\Gamma,\hskip 14.22636ptB=\Sigma A^{\dagger}\Omega

on (2.109) so that the Hermitian conjugation reduction (2.2) is realized. The third condition is satisfied for a diagonal matrix Σ\Sigma by setting

Γ=diag⁡(γ1,γ2,…,γm),\Gamma=\mathrm{diag}(\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots,\gamma_{m}),

where γj\gamma_{j} are real constants. In sections 4 and 5, we apply a binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation and its limiting version to the reduced plane-wave solution, which can maintain the Hermitian conjugation reduction.

To obtain the linear eigenfunction of the Lax-pair representation (2.6) with QQ and RR given by the general plane-wave solution (2.109), we consider a gauge transformation,

Ψ1=P1​e−2​i​t​A​B​𝜳1,Ψ2=i​P2−1​e−i​x​Γ+i​t​Γ2​𝜳2.\displaystyle\Psi_{1}=P_{1}\mathrm{e}^{-2\mathrm{i}tAB}\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{1},\hskip 14.22636pt\Psi_{2}=\mathrm{i}P_{2}^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}x\Gamma+\mathrm{i}t\Gamma^{2}}\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{2}. (2.110)

Then, the Lax-pair representation at ζ=μ\zeta=\mu reduces to the form:

[𝜳1𝜳2]x=i⁡[−μ​IlA−Bμ​Im+Γ]​[𝜳1𝜳2],\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{1}\\ \boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]_{x}=\mathrm{i}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-\mu I_{l}&A\\ -B&\mu I_{m}+\Gamma\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{1}\\ \boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right],
[𝜳1𝜳2]t=i⁡[−2​μ2​Il+A​B2​μ​A−A​Γ−2​μ​B+Γ​B2​μ2​Im+B​A−Γ2]​[𝜳1𝜳2].\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{1}\\ \boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]_{t}=\mathrm{i}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-2\mu^{2}I_{l}+AB&2\mu A-A\Gamma\\ -2\mu B+\Gamma B&2\mu^{2}I_{m}+BA-\Gamma^{2}\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{1}\\ \boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right].

The general solution of this linear system can be expressed using the matrix exponential of an (l+m)×(l+m)(l+m)\times(l+m) matrix as

[𝜳1𝜳2]=ei​x​(𝒁+μ​I)+i​t​(−𝒁2+2​μ2​I)​[𝒞1𝒞2],𝒁⁡(μ):=[−2​μ​IlA−BΓ].\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{1}\\ \boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}x(\boldsymbol{Z}+\mu I)+\mathrm{i}t(-\boldsymbol{Z}^{2}+2\mu^{2}I)}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}{\mathscr{C}}_{1}\\ {\mathscr{C}}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right],\hskip 14.22636pt\boldsymbol{Z}(\mu):=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-2\mu I_{l}&A\\ -B&\Gamma\\ \end{array}\right].

Here, II denotes the identity matrix Il+mI_{l+m} and 𝒞1{\mathscr{C}}_{1} and 𝒞2{\mathscr{C}}_{2} are l×ll\times l and m×lm\times l constant matrices, respectively. Assume that the constant matrix 𝒁⁡(μ)\boldsymbol{Z}(\mu) can be diagonalized as

𝒁​X=X​Λ,Λ:=diag⁡(λ1,λ2,…,λl+m),\boldsymbol{Z}X=X\Lambda,\hskip 14.22636pt\Lambda:=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{l+m}),

using a nonsingular matrix XX whose jjth column is an eigenvector of 𝒁⁡(μ)\boldsymbol{Z}(\mu) with an eigenvalue λj\lambda_{j}. Then, by setting

[𝒞1𝒞2]=X⁡[𝒰1𝒰2],\left[\begin{array}[]{c}{\mathscr{C}}_{1}\\ {\mathscr{C}}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]=X\left[\begin{array}[]{c}{\mathscr{U}}_{1}\\ {\mathscr{U}}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right],

we can compute the matrix exponential in (2.6) explicitly. Thus, in view of (2.110), we obtain

[Ψ1Ψ2]=[P1​e−2​i​t​A​BOOi​P2−1​e−i​x​Γ+i​t​Γ2]​X​ei​x​(Λ+μ​I)+i​t​(−Λ2+2​μ2​I)​[𝒰1𝒰2].\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}P_{1}\mathrm{e}^{-2\mathrm{i}tAB}&O\\ O&\mathrm{i}P_{2}^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}x\Gamma+\mathrm{i}t\Gamma^{2}}\\ \end{array}\right]X\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}x(\Lambda+\mu I)+\mathrm{i}t(-\Lambda^{2}+2\mu^{2}I)}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}{\mathscr{U}}_{1}\\ {\mathscr{U}}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right].

In a similar way, we can also obtain the linear eigenfunction of the adjoint Lax-pair representation (2.7) with the potentials given by (2.109). The constant matrices P1P_{1} and P2P_{2} play no essential role in the Bäcklund–Darboux transformations, i.e., the order of applying a Bäcklund–Darboux transformation and a constant linear transformation using P1P_{1} and P2P_{2} is irrelevant. Thus, in the following, we usually drop P1P_{1} and P2P_{2}, keeping in mind the invariance of the matrix NLS system under the action of the symmetry group.

To express the matrix exponential explicitly, we need to diagonalize the constant matrix 𝒁⁡(μ)\boldsymbol{Z}(\mu); throughout this paper, we do not separately discuss the non-generic case where 𝒁⁡(μ)\boldsymbol{Z}(\mu) is non-diagonalizable (see, e.g., [37]). For a general choice of μ\mu, Γ\Gamma, AA and BB, this requires to solve the characteristic equation for 𝒁⁡(μ)\boldsymbol{Z}(\mu) of degree l+ml+m. Thus, even for the simple case of the two-component vector NLS equation, we generally need to resort to Cardano’s formula [34, 38], which is too complicated for practical purposes. However, as we will see below, with a suitable re-parametrization of μ\mu, Γ\Gamma, AA and BB, it is possible to compute the matrix exponential explicitly without using Cardano’s formula.

3 Dark-soliton solutions

In this section, we apply the elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation defined in Proposition 2.1 to the matrix NLS system (2.1b), which includes the vector NLS system as a special case. Taking a plane-wave solution as the seed solution, we obtain dark-soliton solutions of the multicomponent NLS equations with a self-defocusing or mixed focusing-defocusing nonlinearity. The Hermitian conjugation reduction between the transformed potentials Q~\widetilde{Q} and R~\widetilde{R} can be realized through a suitable choice of the parameters in the solution. In particular, the Bäcklund parameter μ\mu, which has its origin in the spectral parameter ζ\zeta in the Lax-pair representation, is restricted to be real.

3.1 Vector dark soliton without internal degrees of freedom

We first consider the nonreduced vector NLS system, which can be obtained from (2.1b) by setting l=1l=1, Q=𝒒Q=\mbox{\boldmath$q$} and R=𝒓TR=\mbox{\boldmath$r$}^{T}, i.e.

i​𝒒t+𝒒x​x−2​⟨𝒒,𝒓⟩​𝒒=𝟎,\displaystyle{}\mathrm{i}\mbox{\boldmath$q$}_{t}+\mbox{\boldmath$q$}_{xx}-2\langle\mbox{\boldmath$q$},\mbox{\boldmath$r$}\rangle\mbox{\boldmath$q$}=\mbox{\boldmath$0$}, (3.1a)
i​𝒓t−𝒓x​x+2​⟨𝒓,𝒒⟩​𝒓=𝟎.\displaystyle\mathrm{i}\mbox{\boldmath$r$}_{t}-\mbox{\boldmath$r$}_{xx}+2\langle\mbox{\boldmath$r$},\mbox{\boldmath$q$}\rangle\mbox{\boldmath$r$}=\mbox{\boldmath$0$}. (3.1b)

Here, 𝒒:=(q1,…,qm)\mbox{\boldmath$q$}:=(q_{1},\ldots,q_{m}) and 𝒓:=(r1,…,rm)\mbox{\boldmath$r$}:=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{m}) are mm-component row vectors. Note that the simplest case of m=1m=1 corresponds to the scalar NLS system:

i​qt+qx​x−2​q2​r=0,\displaystyle{}\mathrm{i}q_{t}+q_{xx}-2q^{2}r=0, (3.2a)
i​rt−rx​x+2​r2​q=0.\displaystyle\mathrm{i}r_{t}-r_{xx}+2r^{2}q=0. (3.2b)

A general plane-wave solution [21] of the vector NLS system (3.1b) is (cf. (2.109))

qj​(x,t)=aj​ei​γj​x−i⁡(γj2+2​∑k=1mak​bk)​t,rj​(x,t)=bj​e−i​γj​x+i⁡(γj2+2​∑k=1mak​bk)​t,q_{j}(x,t)=a_{j}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\gamma_{j}x-\mathrm{i}\left(\gamma_{j}^{2}+2\sum_{k=1}^{m}a_{k}b_{k}\right)t},\hskip 14.22636ptr_{j}(x,t)=b_{j}\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\gamma_{j}x+\mathrm{i}\left(\gamma_{j}^{2}+2\sum_{k=1}^{m}a_{k}b_{k}\right)t}, (3.3)

where j=1,2,…,mj=1,2,\ldots,m. We consider the generic case where all γj\gamma_{j} are pairwise distinct. The matrix 𝒁⁡(μ)\boldsymbol{Z}(\mu) (cf. (2.6)) in this case is given by

𝒁⁡(μ)=[−2​μa1⋯am−b1γ1O⋮⋱−bmOγm].\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Z}(\mu)=\left[\begin{array}[]{ccccc}-2\mu&a_{1}&\cdots&a_{m}\\ -b_{1}&\gamma_{1}&&\kern-6.0pt\raisebox{-6.0pt}{\mbox{{\Large$O$}}}\\ \vdots&&\ddots&\\ -b_{m}&\mbox{{\Large$O$}}&&\gamma_{m}\\ \end{array}\right].

The characteristic equation (up to an overall sign) reads

det(λ​I−𝒁)=(λ+2​μ)​∏j=1m(λ−γj)+∑k=1mak​bk​∏j≠kj=1m(λ−γj)=0,\displaystyle\det\left(\lambda I-\boldsymbol{Z}\right)=(\lambda+2\mu)\prod_{j=1}^{m}(\lambda-\gamma_{j})+\sum_{k=1}^{m}a_{k}b_{k}\prod_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\scriptstyle j=1}}{{j\neq k}}}^{m}(\lambda-\gamma_{j})=0, (3.8)

which can be rewritten as (cf. [22])

λ+∑k=1mak​bkλ−γk=−2​μ.\displaystyle\lambda+\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{a_{k}b_{k}}{\lambda-\gamma_{k}}=-2\mu. (3.9)

For each eigenvalue λ\lambda that solves (3.9), the corresponding eigenvector is given up to an overall constant as

𝒁⁡(μ)​[1−b1λ−γ1⋮−bmλ−γm]=λ​[1−b1λ−γ1⋮−bmλ−γm].\displaystyle\boldsymbol{Z}(\mu)\left[\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ -\frac{b_{1}}{\lambda-\gamma_{1}}\\ \vdots\\ -\frac{b_{m}}{\lambda-\gamma_{m}}\\ \end{array}\right]=\lambda\left[\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ -\frac{b_{1}}{\lambda-\gamma_{1}}\\ \vdots\\ -\frac{b_{m}}{\lambda-\gamma_{m}}\\ \end{array}\right].

To obtain dark-soliton solutions satisfying a complex conjugation reduction between 𝒒q and 𝒓r, we assume that the parameters γk\gamma_{k}, ak​bka_{k}b_{k} and μ\mu are all real. Then, considering the behavior of the left-hand side of (3.9) as a function of λ\lambda, we can identify conditions for the algebraic equation (3.9) in λ\lambda to have a pair of complex conjugate roots. In particular, at least one of the ak​bka_{k}b_{k} must be positive. Then, among the m+1m+1 solutions of (3.9), we express the pair of complex conjugate roots as λ=ξ±i​η\lambda=\xi\pm\mathrm{i}\eta with η>0\eta>0 to obtain

ξ±i​η+∑k=1mak​bkξ±i​η−γk=−2​μ.\displaystyle\xi\pm\mathrm{i}\eta+\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{a_{k}b_{k}}{\xi\pm\mathrm{i}\eta-\gamma_{k}}=-2\mu. (3.18)

This can be rewritten as

ξ+∑k=1m(ξ−γk)​ak​bk(ξ−γk)2+η2=−2​μ,∑k=1mak​bk(ξ−γk)2+η2=1.\xi+\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{(\xi-\gamma_{k})a_{k}b_{k}}{(\xi-\gamma_{k})^{2}+\eta^{2}}=-2\mu,\hskip 14.22636pt\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{a_{k}b_{k}}{(\xi-\gamma_{k})^{2}+\eta^{2}}=1. (3.19)

Using the second equation, it is in principle possible to determine η(>0)\eta\,(>0) from ξ\xi, γk\gamma_{k} and ak​bka_{k}b_{k} by solving an algebraic equation of degree mm for η2\eta^{2}. Subsequently, the first equation can be used to determine μ\mu from ξ\xi, γk\gamma_{k} and ak​bka_{k}b_{k}. However, in practice, this procedure is not effective for m≥3m\geq 3, because we need to use Cardano’s formula even for m=3m=3.

3.1.1 Scalar NLS equation

It would be instructive to study the scalar NLS system by setting m=1m=1, before considering the multicomponent case. From (3.19), we obtain

2​ξ−γ1=−2​μ,a1​b1=(ξ−γ1)2+η2.2\xi-\gamma_{1}=-2\mu,\hskip 14.22636pta_{1}b_{1}=(\xi-\gamma_{1})^{2}+\eta^{2}. (3.20)

Thus, we have η=a1​b1−(ξ−γ1)2\eta=\sqrt{a_{1}b_{1}-(\xi-\gamma_{1})^{2}} with the condition a1​b1>(ξ−γ1)2a_{1}b_{1}>(\xi-\gamma_{1})^{2} and

𝒁=[2​ξ−γ1a1−b1γ1].\boldsymbol{Z}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}2\xi-\gamma_{1}&a_{1}\\ -b_{1}&\gamma_{1}\\ \end{array}\right].

We choose the eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalues ξ±i​η\xi\pm\mathrm{i}\eta as

𝒁​[a1−ξ±i​η+γ1]=(ξ±i​η)​[a1−ξ±i​η+γ1].\boldsymbol{Z}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}a_{1}\\ -\xi\pm\mathrm{i}\eta+\gamma_{1}\\ \end{array}\right]=(\xi\pm\mathrm{i}\eta)\left[\begin{array}[]{c}a_{1}\\ -\xi\pm\mathrm{i}\eta+\gamma_{1}\\ \end{array}\right].

This solution represents a simple dip in the background plane wave and the asymptotic value at infinity is given as limx→±∞|q⁡(x,t)|=(ξ−γ1)2+η2\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}|q(x,t)|=\sqrt{(\xi-\gamma_{1})^{2}+\eta^{2}}. The elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation defined in Proposition 2.1 does not retain the complex conjugation reduction in general; however, if it is applied to a plane-wave solution in combination with a simple rescaling of the dependent variables, we can realize the complex conjugation reduction in both the old and new pair of variables.

Using Proposition 2.1, we can confirm that the one-dark soliton solution is associated with a bound state of the Lax-pair representation (2.6) at ζ=μ\zeta=\mu, i.e., when the spectral parameter coincides with the parameter of the applied Bäcklund–Darboux transformation. Indeed, the gauge transformation (2.1) provides a generic linear eigenfunction at ζ=μ\zeta=\mu for the transformed potentials as

[Ψ~1Ψ~2]∝|Ψ1(1)Ψ1Ψ2(1)Ψ2|Ψ1(1)​[−q1],\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\widetilde{\Psi}_{1}\\ \widetilde{\Psi}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]\propto\frac{\left|\begin{array}[]{cc}\Psi_{1}^{(1)}&\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}^{(1)}&\Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right|}{\Psi_{1}^{(1)}}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}-q\\ 1\\ \end{array}\right],

up to an overall constant. Here, the superscript (1) means the linear eigenfunction used to define the elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation (2.29). In the above expression, the determinant in the numerator is the Wronskian of two linearly independent eigenfunctions, which is a nonzero constant; q⁡(x,t)q(x,t) in the seed solution is a plane wave and 1/Ψ1(1)1/\Psi_{1}^{(1)} is nonsingular everywhere and decays exponentially fast as x→±∞x\to\pm\infty. Thus, the application of the elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation indeed generates a bound state of the associated linear problem. More generally, the elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation increases the number of bound states by one, by adding a new bound state with a real eigenvalue μ\mu, when it is applied to a seed solution that does not have a bound state at ζ=μ\zeta=\mu. Thus, one can intuitively think of the elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation as a classical analog of the creation operator.

3.1.2 Vector NLS equation

Let us derive a one-dark soliton solution of the vector NLS equation (2.4) in the general mm-component case. Actually, using the elementary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation, we can construct more general solutions of the nonreduced vector NLS system (3.1b), which are not compatible with the complex conjugation reduction; however, such solutions apparently have no physical significance, so we do not discuss them in this paper. Thus, among the general solution (2.6) of the linear problem (2.111) in the vector NLS case, we consider a particular solution,

The vector dark soliton (3.46) has an essentially time-independent shape and contains no free parameters corresponding to the internal degrees of freedom; in the two-component case (m=2m=2), this solution has been extensively studied in the literature [20, 21, 22, 82, 83]. The characteristic polynomial of the square matrix in (3.52) can be written (up to an overall constant) as

Indeed, the 2​l×2​l2l\times 2l eigenvalue problem,

To summarize, a general one-dark soliton solution of the matrix NLS equation (2.5) in the self-defocusing case σ=+1\sigma=+1 can be expressed, up to unitary transformations, as

To express the above solution more explicitly without using the matrix exponential as in (3.2), we need to re-parametrize the matrix BB. We briefly consider the simplest nontrivial case of a 2×22\times 2 Hermitian matrix BB,

4 Vector dark soliton with internal degrees of freedom

In this section, we apply the limiting case of the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation defined in Proposition 2.4 and construct a vector dark-soliton solution with internal degrees of freedom.

We consider the plane-wave solution (3.3) of the vector NLS system (3.1b) in the generic case where the wavenumbers γj\gamma_{j} are pairwise distinct. and

5 Bright-soliton solutions on a plane-wave background

In this section, we apply the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation to the multicomponent NLS equations and obtain their bright-soliton solutions on a general plane-wave background. To simplify the derivation, we use a reduced version of Proposition 2.3, which defines the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation maintaining the Hermitian conjugation reduction between the two matrix dependent variables. In contrast to the construction of the dark-soliton solutions, the Bäcklund parameter μ\mu for generating bright-soliton solutions is complex-valued, i.e., it has a nonzero imaginary part.

Proposition 5.1.

Consider the (l+m)×(l+m)(l+m)\times(l+m) Lax-pair representation for the l×ml\times m matrix NLS equation (2.3) as given by (cf. (2.6) with (2.2))

[Ψ1Ψ2]x=[−i​μ​IlQΣ​Q†​Ωi​μ​Im]​[Ψ1Ψ2],\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]_{x}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-\mathrm{i}\mu I_{l}&Q\\ \Sigma\hskip 1.0ptQ^{\dagger}\hskip 1.0pt\Omega&\mathrm{i}\mu I_{m}\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right],
[Ψ1Ψ2]t=[−2​i​μ2​Il−i​Q​Σ​Q†​Ω2​μ​Q+i​Qx2​μ​Σ​Q†​Ω−i​Σ​Qx†​Ω2​i​μ2​Im+i​Σ​Q†​Ω​Q]​[Ψ1Ψ2].\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]_{t}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-2\mathrm{i}\mu^{2}I_{l}-\mathrm{i}Q\hskip 1.0pt\Sigma\hskip 1.0ptQ^{\dagger}\hskip 1.0pt\Omega&2\mu Q+\mathrm{i}Q_{x}\\ 2\mu\Sigma\hskip 1.0ptQ^{\dagger}\hskip 1.0pt\Omega-\mathrm{i}\Sigma\hskip 1.0ptQ^{\dagger}_{x}\hskip 1.0pt\Omega&2\mathrm{i}\mu^{2}I_{m}+\mathrm{i}\Sigma\hskip 1.0ptQ^{\dagger}\hskip 1.0pt\Omega\hskip 1.0ptQ\\ \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right].

Here, the spectral parameter ζ\zeta is fixed at a complex value μ\mu, Ψ1\Psi_{1} is an l×ll\times l matrix and Ψ2\Psi_{2} is an m×lm\times l matrix; Σ\Sigma and Ω\Omega are m×mm\times m and l×ll\times l diagonal matrices with diagonal entries equal to +1+1 or −1-1. Then, the new potential defined by the formula (see [47, 48] for the scalar case and [49, 34, 50, 38, 77] for the vector case),

Q′\displaystyle Q^{\prime} :=Q+2​i​(μ−μ∗)​Ψ1​(Ψ1†​Ω​Ψ1−Ψ2†​Σ​Ψ2)−1​Ψ2†​Σ,\displaystyle:=Q+2\mathrm{i}(\mu-\mu^{\ast})\Psi_{1}\left(\Psi_{1}^{\dagger}\hskip 1.0pt\Omega\hskip 1.0pt\Psi_{1}-\Psi_{2}^{\dagger}\hskip 1.0pt\Sigma\hskip 1.0pt\Psi_{2}\right)^{-1}\Psi_{2}^{\dagger}\hskip 1.0pt\Sigma,

provides a new solution of the matrix NLS equation (2.3). A linear eigenfunction associated with the new potential Q′Q^{\prime} at the spectral parameter ζ\zeta set equal to μ∗\mu^{\ast} is given by

[Ψ1Ψ2]​(Ψ1†​Ω​Ψ1−Ψ2†​Σ​Ψ2)−1,\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Psi_{1}\\ \Psi_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]\left(\Psi_{1}^{\dagger}\hskip 1.0pt\Omega\hskip 1.0pt\Psi_{1}-\Psi_{2}^{\dagger}\hskip 1.0pt\Sigma\hskip 1.0pt\Psi_{2}\right)^{-1},

which defines a bound state for a proper choice of Ψ1​(μ)\Psi_{1}(\mu) and Ψ2​(μ)\Psi_{2}(\mu).88 8 In some cases, we need to consider a suitable linear combination of the columns in (5.1). Note that the spatial part of the Lax-pair representation Ψx=U​Ψ\Psi_{x}=U\Psi admits the gauge transformation Ψ→ei​k​x​Ψ,U→U+i​k​I\Psi\to\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}\Psi,\;U\to U+\mathrm{i}kI, where kk is an arbitrary complex constant; this transformation is sometimes necessary to obtain a square-integrable eigenfunction. An adjoint linear eigenfunction,

(Ψ1†​Ω​Ψ1−Ψ2†​Σ​Ψ2)−1​[Ψ1†​Ω−Ψ2†​Σ],\displaystyle\left(\Psi_{1}^{\dagger}\hskip 1.0pt\Omega\hskip 1.0pt\Psi_{1}-\Psi_{2}^{\dagger}\hskip 1.0pt\Sigma\hskip 1.0pt\Psi_{2}\right)^{-1}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\!\Psi_{1}^{\dagger}\Omega&\!-\Psi_{2}^{\dagger}\Sigma\end{array}\right],

can provide another bound state at the spectral parameter ζ\zeta equal to μ\mu.99 9 Thus, a multicomponent bright soliton is associated with a pair of bound states: a linear eigenfunction at ζ=μ∗\zeta=\mu^{\ast} and an adjoint linear eigenfunction at ζ=μ\zeta=\mu. For the scalar NLS equation, the adjoint linear eigenfunction can be immediately rewritten as the usual (i.e., column-vector) linear eigenfunction at ζ=μ\zeta=\mu.

This proposition enables us to obtain a formal expression for the bright one-soliton solution on a plane-wave background using the matrix exponential of a constant non-diagonal matrix.

5.1 Matrix bright soliton

We first consider the matrix NLS equation (2.5) for an l×ml\times m matrix QQ, which admits the general plane-wave solution (cf. (2.109)):

Q=e−2​i​t​σ​A​A†​A​ei​x​Γ−i​t​Γ2.\displaystyle Q=\mathrm{e}^{-2\mathrm{i}t\sigma AA^{\dagger}}A\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}x\Gamma-\mathrm{i}t\Gamma^{2}}.

Here, σ=+1\sigma=+1 and σ=−1\sigma=-1 correspond to the self-defocusing case and self-focusing case, respectively; Γ\Gamma is an m×mm\times m real diagonal matrix and AA is an l×ml\times m matrix such that A​A†AA^{\dagger} is a real diagonal matrix. We employ this plane-wave solution as the seed solution and apply the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation defined in Proposition 5.1. Following the procedure described in subsection 2.6, we obtain a new solution of the matrix NLS equation (2.5) in the form:

Q\displaystyle Q =e−2​i​t​σ​A​A†​A​ei​x​Γ−i​t​Γ2+2​i​(μ−μ∗)​Ψ1​(σ​Ψ1†​Ψ1−Ψ2†​Ψ2)−1​Ψ2†\displaystyle=\mathrm{e}^{-2\mathrm{i}t\sigma AA^{\dagger}}A\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}x\Gamma-\mathrm{i}t\Gamma^{2}}+2\mathrm{i}(\mu-\mu^{\ast})\Psi_{1}\left(\sigma\Psi_{1}^{\dagger}\Psi_{1}-\Psi_{2}^{\dagger}\Psi_{2}\right)^{-1}\Psi_{2}^{\dagger}
=e−2​i​t​σ​A​A†​[A+2​(μ−μ∗)​𝜳1​(σ​𝜳1†​𝜳1−𝜳2†​𝜳2)−1​𝜳2†]​ei​x​Γ−i​t​Γ2.\displaystyle=\mathrm{e}^{-2\mathrm{i}t\sigma AA^{\dagger}}\left[A+2(\mu-\mu^{\ast})\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{1}\left(\sigma\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{1}^{\dagger}\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{1}-\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{2}^{\dagger}\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{2}\right)^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{2}^{\dagger}\right]\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}x\Gamma-\mathrm{i}t\Gamma^{2}}. (5.16)

Here, we omit the prime to distinguish the new solution from the old one. In the self-focusing case σ=−1\sigma=-1, the new solution is regular for all xx and tt. The gauge-transformed linear eigenfunction used in (5.16) is given as (cf. (2.6)),

[𝜳1𝜳2]=ei​μ​x+2​i​μ2​t​ei​x​𝒁−i​t​𝒁2​[𝒞1𝒞2],𝒁:=[−2​μ​IlA−σ​A†Γ],\displaystyle\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{1}\\ \boldsymbol{\mathit{\Psi}}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right]=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\mu x+2\mathrm{i}\mu^{2}t}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}x\boldsymbol{Z}-\mathrm{i}t\boldsymbol{Z}^{2}}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}{\mathscr{C}}_{1}\\ {\mathscr{C}}_{2}\\ \end{array}\right],\hskip 14.22636pt\boldsymbol{Z}:=\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}-2\mu I_{l}&A\\ -\sigma A^{\dagger}&\Gamma\\ \end{array}\right],

where 𝒞1{\mathscr{C}}_{1} and 𝒞2{\mathscr{C}}_{2} are l×ll\times l and m×lm\times l constant matrices, respectively. Note that the prefactor ei​μ​x+2​i​μ2​t\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\mu x+2\mathrm{i}\mu^{2}t} plays no role in formula (5.16). This expression is rather formal and appears to be not so useful in the present form for practical applications. Thus, we next consider the simpler case of the vector NLS equation (l=1l=1), particularly targeting on the two-component case (m=2m=2), and obtain a more explicit expression for the solution.

5.2 Vector bright soliton

A general plane-wave solution of the vector NLS equation (2.4) is given by setting bj=σj​aj∗b_{j}=\sigma_{j}a_{j}^{\ast} in (3.3), i.e.

qj​(x,t)\displaystyle q_{j}(x,t) =ajei​γj​x−i⁡(γj2+2​∑k=1mσk​|ak|2)​t,j=1,2,…,m.\displaystyle=a_{j}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\gamma_{j}x-\mathrm{i}\left(\gamma_{j}^{2}+2\sum_{k=1}^{m}\sigma_{k}|a_{k}|^{2}\right)t},\hskip 14.22636ptj=1,2,\ldots,m. (5.23)

Here, we assume that γj​(j=1,2,…,m)\gamma_{j}\;(j=1,2,\ldots,m) are pairwise distinct real constants. We recall the relations (4.1):

2​μ=∑j=1mγj−∑j=1m+1λj\displaystyle 2\mu=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\gamma_{j}-\sum_{j=1}^{m+1}\lambda_{j}

and

σk|ak|2=∏j=1m+1(λj−γk)∏j≠kj=1m(γj−γk),k=1,2,…,m,\displaystyle\sigma_{k}|a_{k}|^{2}=\frac{\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^{m+1}(\lambda_{j}-\gamma_{k})}{\displaystyle\prod_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\scriptstyle j=1}}{{j\neq k}}}^{m}(\gamma_{j}-\gamma_{k})}\hskip 1.0pt,\hskip 14.22636ptk=1,2,\ldots,m, (5.24)

where μ\mu is a complex parameter. Thus, the eigenvalues {λ1,λ2,…,λm+1}\{\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{m+1}\} of the matrix 𝒁⁡(μ)\boldsymbol{Z}(\mu) must satisfy the condition that ∏j=1m+1(λj−γk)\prod_{j=1}^{m+1}(\lambda_{j}-\gamma_{k}) is real-valued for all kk. That is, if we set

λj=ξj+iηj,j=1,2,…,m+1\lambda_{j}=\xi_{j}+\mathrm{i}\eta_{j},\hskip 14.22636ptj=1,2,\ldots,m+1

with real ξj\xi_{j} and ηj\eta_{j}, then we have

∏j=1m+1[(ξj−γk)+iηj]∈ℝ,k=1,2,…,m.\prod_{j=1}^{m+1}\left[(\xi_{j}-\gamma_{k})+\mathrm{i}\eta_{j}\right]\in\mathbb{R},\hskip 14.22636ptk=1,2,\ldots,m.

As mentioned above, considering the range of the complex argument of ∏j=13(λj−γ)\prod_{j=1}^{3}(\lambda_{j}-\gamma) as a function of real γ\gamma, we can establish a correspondence between the configuration of {λ1,λ2,λ3}\{\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}\} and the combination of the signs {σ1,σ2}\{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\}. That is, (i) when ηj>0​(j=1,2,3)\eta_{j}>0\;(j=1,2,3), i.e., all the eigenvalues {λ1,λ2,λ3}\{\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}\} lie in the upper-half plane, we have a self-focusing nonlinearity σ1=σ2=−1\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}=-1; (ii) when η1,η2>0\eta_{1},\eta_{2}>0, −(η1+η2)<η3<0-(\eta_{1}+\eta_{2})<\eta_{3}<0 and Δ>0\Delta>0, we have a mixed focusing-defocusing nonlinearity {σ1,σ2}={+1,−1}\{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\}=\{+1,-1\}; (iii) when η1,η2>0\eta_{1},\eta_{2}>0 and η3<−(η1+η2)\eta_{3}<-(\eta_{1}+\eta_{2}), we have a self-defocusing nonlinearity σ1=σ2=+1\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}=+1; and so on.

When at least one of {σ1,σ2}\{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\} is −1-1, i.e., there exist focusing component(s) in the vector dependent variable, the associated eigenvalue problem is not self-adjoint (cf. subsection 2.2); thus, the bound-state eigenvalues can take complex values. In the self-defocusing case σ1=σ2=+1\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}=+1, the eigenvalue problem is self-adjoint, so the bound-state eigenvalues are restricted to be real; thus, we cannot construct a genuine bright-soliton solution by applying the binary Bäcklund–Darboux transformation used in this section. However, we can obtain a “soliton-like” solution in the self-defocusing case using a complex-valued Bäcklund parameter μ\mu, not associated with a bound state.
